title: Augustus Pardons the Conspirator Cinna
text:
Seneca, writing to the young emperor Nero about mercy, tells a story about Augustus. The emperor learned that Gnaeus Cornelius Cinna, a grandson of Pompey, was plotting to kill him. Augustus spent a restless night, torn between punishing Cinna and sickened by the thought of yet more executions, since earlier conspiracies had been crushed and new ones kept appearing.

Seneca says his wife Livia advised him to do what doctors do: when the usual remedies fail, try the opposite. Severity had not worked, so he should try clemency.

Augustus summoned Cinna alone, told him to listen without interrupting, and then spoke for more than two hours, reminding Cinna of the favors he had received and laying out every detail of the plot. Cinna was speechless. Augustus then told him that he was giving him his life a second time, once as an enemy and now as a plotter, and proposed they become friends.

Later he made Cinna consul. Seneca says Cinna became one of his most loyal friends and left him as his heir, and that no one plotted against Augustus again.
lesson: When punishment keeps producing new enemies, try a different approach. Mercy offered from strength can turn an opponent into an ally.
date: Late 1st century BC or AD 4 (sources differ)
source: Seneca, De Clementia, Book 1, chapter 9; Cassius Dio, Roman History, Book 55, chapters 14 to 22
caveat: Seneca and Cassius Dio disagree about the date and setting, and the long speeches are literary reconstructions.
